newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican rebels not a big issue in Clinton visit.
newsitem.headline: Mexican rebels not a big issue in Clinton visit.

text.p: When President Bill Clinton visits his Mexican counterpart this week, both leaders are likely to ignore a latent threat in the south of Mexico -- guerrilla revolt.

Across Mexico's impoverished south, pockets of guerrilla resistance have sprung up in the last three years that President Ernesto Zedillo will try to sweep under the red carpet he is rolling out for Clinton.

In a list of themes both governments are due to discuss during Clinton's May 5-7 visit, there was no mention of counter-insurgency cooperation. Drugs, immigration and trade are the main items on the agenda.
The rebels, a rag-tag band of landless Indians and peasants led by a handful of media-savvy Marxists, barely represent a military threat in Mexico, and they operate in mountains far from the capital.

But they have taken a stand against issues that form the bedrock of U.S.-Mexican cooperation -- the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) that they say has turned southern Mexico into a forgotten backwater, and the militarization of the region, ostensibly to fight drug trafficking.

Analysts say there is a growing underclass in southern Mexico who are the NAFTA losers, lacking access to jobs in the shiny new export plants that dot the north of the country and increasingly squeezed out of traditional farming by a drive toward modern agriculture.

It was no coincidence that the first rebel uprising by the Zapatista National Liberation Army was launched on Jan. 1, 1994, the day the NAFTA treaty took effect between the United States, Mexico and Canada.
The Zapatistas called NAFTA a "death sentence" for the poor Indian communities in the southeastern state of Chiapas where they operate.

In June last year, another rebel group called the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) sprung up chiefly in the states of Guerrero and Oaxaca, hostile to the United States and doggedly Marxist. Its units operate over a swathe of southern Mexico, evading a huge military clampdown.
"What worries me is that these type of phenomena are multiplying," Roberto Blum, a political scientist at the Centre of Development Investigations in Mexico City, told Reuters.
"No rebel group is a threat in itself...but the problem is that when they multiply, there is the perception that the government is losing control."
However, he said Washington -- which was obsessed with left-wing guerrillas in Central America in the 1980s -- was likely to largely shrug off the rebel threat in Mexico.
"The U.S. government thinks that at this time, helping the government will remove the problems in the south," he said.

He said such a strategy could work, providing Mexico's Institutional Revolutionary Party, which has ruled Mexico for 68 years, allowed clean mid-term elections this year. "If the elections are not clean, that will give greater strength to these violent groups," he said.
Zedillo has launched a campaign that has fairly effectively kept the guerrillas out of sight and out of mind since the EPR launched attacks in which some 20 people died last August.
Thousands of troops and armoured vehicles have rumbled into suspected EPR areas, and suspected ringleaders have been seized, though many claim charges against them are difficult to substantiate.

In Chiapas, Zedillo has partially neutralised the appeal of the media-friendly Zapatistas by surrounding them in their mountain strongholds with a military cordon, and making little effort to re-start stalled peace talks.

Recently, the government has also started expelling foreign human rights workers seeking to publicise abuses in areas of rebel support. Eleven Europeans were fighting expulsion this weekend, and one American and two Central Americans were thrown out of the country in April.
